{
    "id": "15-orchestration/backpressure-handling",
    "title": "Backpressure Handling",
    "category": "15-orchestration",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Detect and shed or buffer load when downstream consumers fall behind, using explicit queue limits, load-shedding policies, and honest propagation instead of unbounded queues.",
    "body": "Backpressure Handling Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Backpressure is the system admitting it is saturated instead of hiding the lag in a growing queue. The skill covers measuring consumer lag against explicit thresholds, choosing the response per queue type: bounded buffers for bursty-but-must-complete work, immediate shedding for latency-sensitive work, and degradation for work that has cheaper fallbacks. Pressure is propagated to callers honestly, because a lie here becomes a timeout there. When to Use Use when producers can outrun consumers: agent fleets, ingestion pipelines, or request handlers where queue growth is worse than refusal. Do not respond to saturation with an unbounded queue. It converts a visible overload into an invisible one that eventually fails bigger and later. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Depth, arrival rate, and consumption rate per queue | | | | Yes | Thresholds and the response per queue type: buffer, shed, or degrade | | | | No | Degraded-mode responses available when shedding is undesirable | Procedure 1. Instrument every queue with depth and arrival and consumption rates before tuning anything. 2. Classify each queue: must-complete, latency-sensitive, or degradable. 3. Set explicit thresholds for each queue marking normal, pressured, and saturated states. 4. Respond by class: bounded buffer, immediate shed with a clear refusal, or degraded fallback. 5. Propagate pres sure upstream honestly so callers can slow down instead of guessing. 6. Alert on sustained pressure, not transient bursts, and record shed decisions for review. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Per-queue state: normal, pressured, or saturated | | | | What was shed or degraded, with reasons | | | | Signals sent upstream to slow producers | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Invisible overload | Unbounded queues hide growing lag | Bound every queue and alarm on depth | | Shedding the wrong work | Uniform drop policy sheds critical requests | Classify queues and shed per policy | | Silent degradation | Fallbacks served without disclosure | Mark degraded responses so callers can react | | Pressure not propagated | Producers keep full send rate | Propagate explicit slow-down signals upstream | | Threshold thrash | Alarm flapping at the boundary | Hysteresis between pressured and normal states | Security and Authority Boundary Load shedding changes what work a system accepts, which is a policy decision with user impact. Keep shed policies in configuration with review, log what is refused, and never shed security-relevant work such as audit events or authentication under load. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Apache Kafka documentation on consumer lag and flo w control semantics (https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/). 2. The Project Reactor reactive library with bounded buffering (https://projectreactor.io/). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. {
    "id": "15-orchestration/capability-based-skill-selection",
    "title": "Capability-Based Skill Selection",
    "category": "15-orchestration",
    "level": "advanced",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Select and sequence canonical skills for a task by matching required capabilities, discriminating competing candidates, checking eligibility and dependencies, and using execution evidence to choose the next skill.",
    "body": "Capability-Based Skill Selection Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Capability-based skill selection turns a task into an explicit skill decision rather than treating retrieval as selection. It identifies the capabilities required by the current task, compares competing canonical skills, checks evidence, compatibility, authority, and prerequisites, then selects an executable skill and determines what should happen next from the observed result. This skill is intended for agent runtimes and orchestrators that consume a canonical skill registry. It does not replace search, the registry, dependency graph, or execution runtime. When to Use Use when an agent must decide which skill to invoke for a concrete task and more than one plausible skill may match. Do not use this as a substitute for simple deterministic lookup when the canonical skill ID is already known. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | / | Yes | Current task, objective, or unresolved subtask | | | | Yes | Project state, constraints, environment, prior results, and available tools | | | | Yes | Candidate canonical skills discovered from the registry/search boundary | | | | No | Required capabilities already inferred by an upstream goal/capability resolver | | | | No | Skills already executed successful ly for the current task | | | | No | Available benchmark, provenance, freshness, compatibility, or runtime evidence | Selection Procedure 1. Normalize the task into the capabilities required to make progress. 2. Resolve candidate skills through the canonical registry and reject unknown or non-canonical IDs. 3. Separate direct matches from merely related skills. 4. Compare competing candidates using task fit, required capability coverage, eligibility, compatibility, evidence quality, freshness, and known limitations. 5. Resolve mandatory prerequisites before selecting a dependent skill. 6. Prefer the smallest sufficient skill set; do not select skills merely because they are related. 7. Produce an explicit selection rationale and rejected-candidate reasons. 8. Invoke the selected executable skill only when its prerequisites and authority conditions are satisfied. 9. Verify the result against the task acceptance criteria. 10. If verification fails, classify the failure and select the next justified skill or recovery action rather than blindly repeating the same invocation. 11. Stop when the task is verified complete, blocked by an external condition, or requires escalation. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Canonical skill ID/version selected for the current step | | | | Dependencies that must be satisfied before invocation | | | | Plausible candidates rejected with explicit reasons | | | | Next invocation, verification, recovery, escalation, or terminal decision | | | | Evidence needed to verify the selected action | | | | , , or | Decision Contract A valid selection must answer all of these questions: - What capability is required now? - Which canonical skill satisfies it? - Why is it better than the competing candidates? - Which prerequisites must run first? - Is the skill eligible in the current context? - What evidence will verify the invocation? - What result causes the agent to invoke the next skill? - What result causes recovery, substitution, escalation, or termination? A skill must not be selected solely because it contains matching keywords. Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Retrieval mistaken for selection | Top search result is treated as authoritative | Evaluate competing candidates against task requirements | | Ambiguous candidates | Several skills satisfy overlapping capabilities | Require explicit discrimination reasons and tie-break evidence | | Hidden prerequisite | Dependent skill selected before required capability exists | Resolve prerequisite/dependency graph before invocation | | Stale or weak evidence | Candidate has outdated or insufficient proof | Prefer fresher, provenance-backed evidence and surface the gap | | Ineligible candidate | Compatibility, authority, or runtime constraints are unmet | Reject candidate and continue with an eligible alternative | | Repeated failed invocation | Same action is retried without new evidence | Classify failure and choose recovery, substitution, or escalation | | Premature completion | Selection succeeds but task outcome is unverified | Req uire outcome evidence before | | Over-selection | Agent invokes related skills without causal need | Select the smallest sufficient skill set | Security and Authority Boundary Skill selection does not grant permissions. The selected skill must execute only within its declared authority, security boundary, compatibility constraints, and available runtime permissions. High-impact or irreversible actions must remain subject to the governing approval and policy controls of the consuming agent runtime. Evidence This skill is motivated by two complementary evidence classes: 1. Public demand signals around automated task breakdown, agent orchestration, and assignment based on skills/performance. 2. Skills Tree's current behavioral evaluation gap: retrieval quality is now measured, but task-specific skill discrimination, dependency-aware selection, invocation, and next-skill decisions are not yet comprehensively benchmarked. The demand evidence is recorded in ; it is not treated as popularity or adoption data. {
    "id": "15-orchestration/circuit-breaking",
    "title": "Circuit Breaking",
    "category": "15-orchestration",
    "level": "advanced",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Stop calling a failing dependency after a threshold, fail fast while the circuit is open, and probe with trial calls before closing so one slow or broken service cannot take the caller down with it.",
    "body": "Circuit Breaking Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Retries have a limit beyond which they become part of the outage. A circuit breaker converts persistent failure into a fast, local decision: after a threshold of consecutive failures the circuit opens and calls short-circuit immediately; after a reset window a limited probe tests the water; only a successful probe closes the circuit again. The caller sheds load and stays responsive while the dependency recovers. When to Use Use around any remote dependency whose failure or latency can exhaust the caller — model APIs, databases, downstream services called on a request path. Do not wrap workloads where every call must succeed; a breaker that skips required work turns degraded mode into silent data loss. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The dependency the breaker guards | | | | Yes | Consecutive failures that open the circuit | | | | Yes | Open period before a probe is allowed | | | | Yes | The single trial call used in half-open state | Procedure 1. Track consecutive failures per dependency, not globally; one bad endpoint should not open every circuit. 2. When the count reaches the threshold, open the circuit and fail fast — no call, no queue, no waiting. 3. While open, answer immediately with a defined degradation result, never with an exception shape callers have not agreed to. 4. After the reset timeout, m ove to half-open and allow exactly one probe call; the rest still fail fast. 5. Close on a successful probe and reset the counter; re-open and restart the timer on a failed probe. 6. Export circuit state as a metric; state transitions are the outage narrative. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Current circuit state | | | | What the breaker did with this call | | | | Consecutive failures at decision time | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Flapping | Threshold or timeout tuned to noise | Calibrate to the dependency's real error profile | | No half-open state | Open circuits close on faith after the timer | Require one successful probe before closing | | Shared breakers | One circuit for heterogeneous calls | Track per dependency and per call class | | State lost on restart | Counters held in process memory only | Persist or re-warm counters; treat restart as probe | | Silent degradation | Short-circuits invisible to callers and operators | Export state metrics and log every transition | Security and Authority Boundary The breaker protects the caller's time and threads; it does not repair the dependency or verify its recovery. Post-incident validation of the dependency stays with its owner, and an open circuit is a degraded state, never a healthy one. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Circuit Breaker pattern on microservices.io (https://microservices.io/patterns/reliability/circuit-breaker.html). 2. Wikipedia's overview of fault tolerance (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fault_tolerance). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. Related Skills - Retry Backoff — the bounded retry layer the breaker sits behind. - Event Triggers — event paths where fast failure must not silently drop triggers.     "body": "Cross-Agent Locking Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description When two agents can mutate the same resource, correctness needs a lock, and distributed locks need more than mutual exclusion. The skill covers choosing lock granularity, issuing time-bounded leases with fencing tokens so a stalled holder cannot corrupt later writers, ordering acquisition to prevent deadlock, and handling the crash case: leases expire, the next holder proceeds, and the fencing token rejects the zombie. Lock state lives in a coordinator both sides can see, never in agent memory. When to Use Use when multiple agents operate on shared state or resources that must not be mutated concurrently: shared files, external accounts, or single-instance workflows. Do not treat advisory flags in a shared document as locks. Without a coordinator, expiry, and fencing, two agents will both believe they hold the resource. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Identifier of the shared resource to protect | | | | Yes | Maximum lease duration before forced expiry | | | | Yes | Shared lease store both acquiring agents can observe | Procedure 1. Choose lock granularity: the smallest scope that prevents the conflict, not the whole task. 2. Acquire a lease from the coordinator with a bounded TTL and a fencing token number. 3. Record the token with every mutation so stale writes can be rejected downstream. 4. Acquire multiple locks in a fixed global order to prevent deadlock cyc les. 5. Release the lease immediately after the critical section; never hold across waits. 6. Handle expiry: renew in-flight if needed, and accept rejection when a higher token exists. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Holder identity, token, TTL, and expiry time | | | | Ordered acquisition and release events | | | | Contested acquisitions and fencing rejections | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Split-brain hold | Lease expiry unobserved by a stalled holder | Fencing tokens rejected at the resource | | Deadlock | Locks acquired in different orders | Fixed global acquisition order | | Lock leak | Crashed agent never released | Bounded TTL with automatic expiry | | Over-broad locking | Whole-task locks serialize everything | Lock the smallest conflicting scope | | Advisory lock ignored | A rogue agent bypasses the coordinator | Enforce at the resource with token checks, not trust | Security and Authority Boundary Lock coordinators become shared infrastructure with availability impact.     "body": "Dead-Letter Queuing Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Some messages cannot be processed, and retrying them forever converts one bad payload into a stuck pipeline. Dead-letter queuing draws the line: after a bounded number of attempts, the message moves to a dedicated dead-letter queue carrying its attempts, errors, and original payload. The main queue keeps flowing, the failure stays inspectable, and a replay path exists for after the cause is fixed. When to Use Use with any task queue or event pipeline where a malformed or failing message must not block subsequent messages. Do not use a dead-letter queue as a trash bin: entries are quarantined pending diagnosis, and unbounded growth without review hides an outage in plain sight. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The message being processed | | | | Yes | Processing attempts before dead-lettering | | | | Yes | Prior failures for this message id | | | | Yes | The dead-letter destination with its metadata schema | Procedure 1. Track attempts per message id; the count travels with the message, not with worker memory. 2. On each failure, record the error and timestamp; retry only while under the attempt bound. 3. At the bound, move the message to the dead-letter queue with its payload, attempts, and error history attached. 4. Surface dead-letter depth and entry age as operational alarms; a growing dead-letter queue is a failing pipeline. 5. Diagnose entries before replay: fix the consumer or correct the payload, then replay deliberately. 6. Re-run replayed messages through the same accounting so a still-failing replay dead-letters again, visibly.     "description": "Carry one absolute end-time deadline through every orchestration hop so each step budgets its remaining time, children inherit a tightened deadline, and late results are discarded rather than delivered.",
    "body": "Deadline Propagation Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Relative timeouts do not compose: three sequential steps with a 5-second timeout each can stall a caller for 15 seconds. Deadline propagation fixes the arithmetic by carrying one absolute end time: each hop computes remaining time against the same clock, children receive the tighter of their own budget and the parent's remaining time, and results that arrive after the deadline are discarded instead of patched into the run late. When to Use Use in any multi-hop orchestration — service calls, subagent trees, pipelines — where a caller's total wait must stay bounded. Do not substitute per-hop timeouts without checking the sum; a chain of local limits is not a global one. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The absolute end time for the whole run | | | | Yes | Injectable current time for deterministic decisions | | | | No | The step's own preferred local budget | | | | No | Downstream hops inheriting the deadline | Procedure 1. Set one absolute deadline at run start, from the caller's wall-clock budget; it is a timestamp, not a duration. 2. At each hop, compute remaining time as deadline minus now; a hop with no remaining time fails fast without starting. 3. Give each child the tighter of its own budget and the parent's remaining time minus the parent's reserve. 4. Reject late results even if they eventua lly complete; a result after the deadline is not a result for this run. 5. Record per-step time consumption so postmortems can show where the budget went. 6. Reserve a margin for serialization and cleanup; a deadline with no reserve fails at the packaging step. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Time left at the decision point | | | | The tightened deadline handed to a child | | | | Whether the step or result is usable | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Relative-only budgets | Per-step timeouts whose sum exceeds the caller's budget | Propagate one absolute deadline | | Deadline-blind queues | Enqueued work starts without checking the clock | Check remaining time at dequeue, not just enqueue | | Children outliving parents | Children keep their local budget after the parent expired | Hand children the tighter of own budget and parent remaining | | Late results accepted | Stragglers patched in after expiry | Classify post-deadline results as late and discard | | No time accounting | Postmortems cannot say where time went | Record per-step consumption against budget | Security and Authority Boundary Deadline propagation bounds wall-clock time; it does not certify the quality of what was rushed to fit. When to Use Use when multi-agent or multi-node execution must survive worker failure without losing workflow progress, or when several workers need a consistent view of shared state. Serialize updates with a deterministic order: sequence numbers or version vectors, never wall clocks. 4. Replicate each update and declare durability onl y after quorum acknowledgment. 5. Merge concurrent updates with a deterministic conflict rule so replicas converge. 6. Recover failed workers by rebuilding their state from the acknowledged replica log. {
    "id": "15-orchestration/idempotency-keys",
    "title": "Idempotency Keys",
    "category": "15-orchestration",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Assign client-generated idempotency keys to state-changing requests so retries and at-least-once delivery produce one effect, with duplicate calls returning the recorded first result.",
    "body": "Idempotency Keys Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description At-least-once delivery means the same request will sometimes arrive twice; idempotency keys turn that from a bug into a non-event. The client attaches a unique key to each operation intent, the server checks the key before executing, and a replayed key returns the stored first response instead of executing again. The stored response plus a payload fingerprint closes the gap between \"same key\" and \"same request\". When to Use Use for any state-changing request that may be retried — payment calls, task creation, webhook handlers, queue consumers under at-least-once semantics. Do not bother for pure reads or naturally idempotent operations; the machinery earns its cost only where duplicates have effects. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Client-generated unique key for this operation intent | | | | Yes | Digest of the payload the key refers to | | | | Yes | Server-side record of executed keys | | | | Yes | How long replayed keys resolve to stored results | Procedure 1. Generate the key client-side, unique per operation intent — not per session, not per process. 2. Before executing, look the key up: a hit with a matching fingerprint returns the stored response; a hit with a mismatching fingerprint is an error. 3. On a miss, execute once, then store the response keyed by the key and fingerprint. 4. Keep the TTL at least as long as the client's longest retry window; shorter expiry quietly reintroduces duplicates. 5. Keep keys out of URLs and logs; they identify operations and may correlate to sensitive intents. 6. Treat in-flight keys as locked: concurrent duplicate calls wait for the first execution rather than racing it. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The first execution's response, returned on every replay | | | | Whether this call returned a stored result | | | | When the key record expires | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Key reuse across payloads | Same key sent with different request bodies | Store and compare a payload fingerprint | | Server-generated keys | Key minted per attempt, not per intent | Generate the key client-side per operation intent | | No stored response | Key existence recorded, result discarded | Store the response, not just the key | | TTL shorter than retries | Key expires while the client is still retrying | Keep the TTL above the retry window | | Keys in URLs | Idempotency keys landing in access logs | Send keys in headers or bodies, never the path | Security and Authority Boundary Idempotency protects the server's effect from duplication; it does not order distinct operations. Sequencing two dif ferent calls — even related ones — needs explicit ordering, which this skill does not provide. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1.     "description": "Maintain a persistent, file-backed Kanban board as the shared source of task truth between a coding agent, its orchestrator, and a human reviewer: an explicit task lifecycle with receipted transitions, a blocked-by dependency DAG with a derived ready set, and a per-task merge gate whose completion evidence is verified before a task may be marked done.",
    "body": "Category: Orchestration Skill Level: Intermediate Stability: experimental Version: v1 Added: 2026-10 Last Updated: 2026-10 Description Kanban task management gives an agent a durable board it can read and mutate between sessions instead of holding the plan in context. The board is plain files under version control in the repository being worked, so task state survives crashes, context resets, and handoffs between agents and humans. This page defines a portable contract for lifecycle, dependencies, concurrency, and completion evidence; concrete implementations are references, not requirements. The Portable Contract Any conforming implementation must provide: - Board store: task records stored as files inside the repository (or a directory the repository's review surface can see). Never a side-channel database a code review cannot diff. - Task record: stable ID, status, summary, tags, edges (referencing other task IDs), an append-only list of transition receipts, and evidence references (commit SHAs, merge receipts). - Transition receipts: every status change must append a receipt (timestamp, old→new status, human-readable response message, optional evidence). Receipts are never rewritten or de leted. - Controller CLI: the only writer. Mutations happen through controller commands; direct hand-edits of board files are out-of-contract (see Concurrency Model). - Derived ready set: a query that returns, without mutating anything, the tasks an agent may legally pick up next (status eligible and all targets satisfied per the semantics below). Task Lifecycle: Legal and Illegal Transitions States: , plus (soft, orthogonal) and (a flag on , not a fifth state). | Transition | Legal? | Rule | |---|---|---| | | ✅ | Planning step; receipt required | | | ✅ | Fast-track pick; receipt required | | | ✅ | Only from the ready set (all blockers satisfied); receipt required | | | ✅ | Only if the task's merge gate is satisfied (see Completion Evidence); receipt + evidence | | | ✅ | Return: work stopped; receipt must say why | | | ✅ | Re-plan; receipt required | | | ✅ | Reopen: new receipt citing the defect/omission; prior receipts retained; task re-enters ready computation | | , | ❌ | Reopen must pass through so an owner takes the task again | | | ❌ | Skips execution evidence and the gate | | any → | ✅ | Soft archive: history and receipts stay queryable; never a delete | | | ✅ | Restore: new receipt; dependency edges re-validated against current IDs | | | ❌ | Restore first, then execute the normal gate | | any transition | ❌ | Without a response receipt, or via a hand-edit instead of the controller | Setting/clearing the flag on is always legal with a receipt; a blocked task leaves the ready set until cleared. Blocked-By Dependency Semantics Edges are validated at write time and re-valida ted by every ready-set computation: | Blocker state | Semantics | |---|---| | (completed) | Satisfied — does not gate the dependent task | | | Does not gate, but the controller emits a warning receipt | | Missing ID | Rejected at edge-creation time. If discovered later, the edge is unresolved: the dependent task is not ready and a validation error is surfaced | | Cyclic | Rejected at creation by cycle check over the DAG; late-discovered cycles make all members not-ready | | / / | Gates normally until the blocker reaches or | The ready set is always recomputed from the live DAG — cached orderings are never trusted. Concurrency Model Read-before-mutate is not concurrency control: two agents can both read the same state and then both write, losing one transition. The contract prescribes exactly one of: 1. Single controller: one controller process owns the board and serializes mutations, or 2. Optimistic CAS: every mutation carries the content hash of the board state it was computed against; on mismatch the controller aborts and the agent re-reads. Hand-edited board files are detected as drift and must be reconciled through the controller.     "body": "Result Aggregation Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Parallel execution multiplies results and failure shapes at the same time. Aggregation turns a cloud of futures into one report: each task contributes a (id, status, output) tuple, missing tasks appear as missing instead of vanishing, and the merge order is deterministic. The aggregate carries per-task provenance, so any claim in the combined output can be traced back to the task that produced it. When to Use Use whenever work is split across parallel subagents or workers and the caller needs one combined, trustworthy answer. Do not use unordered ad-hoc merging; a merge that depends on arrival order produces a different output on every run. Register the full expected task id set at dispatch time; the plan, not the arrival count, defines completeness. 2. Collect results as (id, status, output) tuples; failures are results, not exceptions to swallow. 3. On aggregation, subtract completed ids from expected ids; anything unaccounted is missing — with the timeout recorded. 4. Apply the merge policy per status: include completed, recor d failed, mark missing; the policy decides what missing means for the whole. 5. Merge in task id order, never arrival order, so identical inputs produce identical output. 6. Emit the aggregate with per-task provenance: which task produced which part of the combined result.     "body": "Workflow Versioning Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A workflow definition is code that runs many times. Versioning it explicitly — semantic bumps, a recorded version per execution, and a written rule for what counts as compatible — separates \"the run behaved as defined\" from \"the definition changed underneath the run\". Executions carry their definition version, so a result can always be traced to the exact steps that produced it. When to Use Use whenever a multi-step workflow runs repeatedly and its steps, prompts, tool wiring, or output schema may change over time. Do not use one mutable definition with in-place edits; every execution should be able to name the version that produced it. Assign each definition an explicit version; an unversioned definition is a defect, not a default. 2. Classify every change against the written rule: step removal, output schema change, or semantic edits are breaking; additive steps are additive; wording fixes are fixes. 3. Record the definition version inside every execution at start; a result without a version cannot be interpreted later. 4. Pin in-flight executions to the version they started with; migrate only between runs, never during one. 5. For breaking bumps, provide an explicit migration or a compatibility window; never change a version in place. 6. Keep the definition history queryable so any past result can be replayed against its own version.
